en: go, alight on the slopes, on the hills,
where, warm and soft, there breathe their fragrance
the sweet breezes of the native soil!
Greet the banks of the Jordan,
O my homeland, so beautiful and lost!
O remembrance, so dear and fatal!
Golden harp of the prophetic seers,
why do you hang mute from the willow?
Rekindle the memories in our breast,
speak to us of the time that was!
Either, like the fates of Solyma,
draw forth a sound of harsh lament,
or may the Lord inspire in you a harmony
that may instil in us strength to endure suffering!
notes: The source file names Edward Downes as translator; this English is a new line-by-line translation of the Italian, not his.
line 1.3-4: literally 'where are fragrant, warm and soft, / the sweet airs of the native soil'; 'aure' are breezes or airs.
line 2.4: 'membranza' is a poetic form of 'rimembranza' (remembrance, memory); 'fatal' is 'fateful' as well as 'deadly', the memory bound up with their fate.
line 3.1: 'vati' are poet-prophets (Latin vates); 'fatidici' means prophetic, foretelling fate. The harp hanging on the willow recalls Psalm 137.
line 3.3-4: 'raccendi' and 'favella' are imperatives addressed to the harp; 'ci' is 'to us'.

line 4.1: 'Sòlima' is Solyma, an old poetic name for Jerusalem. The phrase 'O simile di Sòlima ai fati' is compressed: 'either, like [one who sings] the fates of Jerusalem' or 'either, in keeping with Jerusalem's fate'; readings differ.
line 4.2: 'crudo' is raw, harsh or bitter.
line 4.3: 'concento' is a harmony or concord of sounds.
line 4.4: 'virtù' here is strength or fortitude (the power to bear 'il patire', suffering); 'ne' is 'in us'.
